title: The Kettle
passages:
The Marrow drew alongside the Kettle's low gate and Sol cut the engine. The sudden quiet left a hollow in the air, filled by the creak of lashed pallets and the slap of water against rotting hulls. The Kettle was the arcology's low gate, a warrens of docks where the waterline sucked at everything not tied down. Sol heaved the bow line over a bollard and made it fast, the rope biting into her palms.

Dey lay on the deck mat where she'd dropped him after the last dive. His chest rose in shallow, rattling pulls, each breath sounding like it was being dragged through gravel. His dive harness lay beside him, scrubber canister cracked open, useless. Sol had already stripped him out of his suit, but she couldn't strip the cold out of his lungs or the salt out of his eyes.

Pru Quill stepped over the gunwale, the berth book tucked under one arm. It was a heavy ledger, bound in leather gone stiff with salt, pages swollen at the edges. She didn't offer a greeting. She opened it to the current season and ran a finger down the column.

"Six berths left," Quill said. "That's all. Six names above the waterline before the storm bell shuts the channel for the season."

Sol leaned against the mast. "And if one of those six stays empty?"

"Then my own berth is forfeit," Quill said. "I don't get to shade the number. I can't lie. The book says six, I say six."

Dey coughed into his elbow, a wet, racking sound. He turned his head on the mat. "You came all the way out here to tell us you're desperate?"

"I came to name the price," Quill said. "That's my job. You wanted berths above the waterline. Here's the count. Take it, or the water takes you."

Sol glanced at Dey. His face was gray under the salt stubble, his lips blue at the corners. He was breathing faster now, shallow and fast, one hand clutching his side like he could hold his ribs together. "He's not cargo," Sol said. "He's crew."

"Then he's a name," Quill said. "Six names. Six crates of medicine. That's what the book wants."

A line snapped somewhere down the dock, and a salvaged trawler slammed against its mooring with a hollow thud. The wind shifted, bringing the smell of diesel and wet cordage. Sol pushed off the mast and knelt beside the mat.

"Six," Sol said quietly. "We can do six."

Quill closed the book with a dull thud. "The bell starts its count at the turn of the tide. You have until then."

She stepped back onto the dock, and the wood groaned under her weight. Sol looked down at Dey. His eyes were open, glassy, tracking her.

"You hear that?" Sol said. "Six berths. We're buying them all."

Dey managed a thin, wet laugh. "Of course you are. And who's the sixth name?"

Dey's question lands like a stone on wet wood. Quill doesn't look at him. She looks at Sol.

"The indenture," Quill says. "One name, bound to the Kettle until the debt works out. Yours, Dey Okafor. Six crates and your signature. That's the price for six berths."

Sol is on her feet before the last syllable. She steps between Quill and the mat, her body blocking the view, her hand coming up like she can cup Dey's ears shut. "Don't say it like he's here to hear it."

"I am here," Dey says. His voice is thin, rattling, but it carries. "Quit it, Sol. I'm not a child. Take your hand off my head."

Sol's fingers hover an inch above his salt-crusted hair. She doesn't touch him, but she doesn't step back either. "You're not signing anything."

"Someone has to," Dey says. "You want six names? I'm a name. I've been diving to buy back my freedom since I was sixteen, and now you're telling me the price is my freedom? That's rich."

"It's not freedom," Quill says. She can't soften it. She can't blink away the sharp edge. "It's an indenture. You work the debt off on the docks until the Factor's books balance. I don't set the terms. I just read them."

"You read them to my face," Dey says. "Why don't you just spit on me and get it over with?"

"Because spitting isn't in the berth book," Quill says. "Signing is."

Sol looks down at him. Dey's chest is heaving, each breath a wet scrap against his ribs, but his eyes are clear enough to cut. He grips the edge of the mat with one hand, knuckles white.

"You don't have to do this," Sol says.

"Someone does," Dey says. "Unless you've got six crates of medicine and a spare soul in your pocket. Hand me the pen, Quill. Let's see how the indenture reads."

Quill opens the book again. The pages are swollen, the ink dark. She holds out a stylus, the kind dock-wardens use to etch names into the leather so the salt can't wash them out.

Dey lifts his head from the mat. His breath whistles through his nose. "Go on," he says to Sol. "Cover my ears again. See if it changes the price."

Sol doesn't move. She looks at Quill, then at the stylus, then at Dey's face — gray, stubborn, alive.

"That's what I thought," Dey says.

The dock creaks. Somewhere on the frame, metal clamps into metal. The air feels like it's holding its breath.

Quill says, "Six crates. One name. The tide turns in forty minutes. That's all the time the book gives us."

Dey lets his head fall back onto the mat. "Forty minutes," he says. "Funny. That's almost enough time to change your mind."

Sol doesn't answer. She stares at the indenture line in the book, waiting to see whose hand will reach for it first.
